title: Streaming metrics ingest: failover and backpressure strategy for Console
creator: Aisha Kaur
description:
Goal: Design and implement a robust real-time ingest path for Console metrics that tolerates downstream slowness and transient failures while preserving per-tenant ordering guarantees and low tail latency. Scope covers the queue/stream processors, consumer-side backpressure, failover strategies for processor instances, partitioning scheme, and operational signals exposed to the Console UI and alerts.

Background: Our Console telemetry is moving to a real-time streaming model to power live dashboards, route-level latency heatmaps, per-token cost breakdowns, and rollout traces. Current prototype uses a single Kafka topic with a fixed partitioning by customer ID, and a stateless consumer group in the metrics-ingest service. This has surfaced two classes of issues in load tests: 1) hotspotting when a few tenants produce high event volumes; 2) capacity collapse when downstream enrichment processors or analytics sinks slow down, leading to large consumer lag and memory pressure.

Proposed design highlights: 
- Dynamic tenant-aware sharding: route incoming events into virtual shards based on a hashed (customer_id + route_id) key but allow shard rebalancing at runtime. This reduces long-lived hot partitions by splitting heavy tenants across multiple shards when thresholds are exceeded.
- Per-shard at-least-once ingestion with idempotent downstream writes: keep sequence metadata (event_id, shard_seq) on events and require sinks (clickhouse/OLAP buffer) to deduplicate by event_id for idempotency.
- Consumer-side backpressure using a two-layer buffering model: small in-memory per-shard ring buffers for low-latency flow; a bounded local spill-to-disk queue per instance for surge protection. When local queues fill, emit tenant-level backpressure markers to the router so producers can throttle or reroute to burst capacity.
- Graceful failover and ownership handoff: use a lightweight lease service backed by our control-plane datastore for shard leases. On instance termination, a short handoff window allows checkpoint pushing; if no handoff, the new owner resumes from last committed offset with idempotent reprocessing.
- Prioritization & QoS: mark events by priority (critical, normal, sample) and ensure that user-facing real-time dashboards get higher priority treatment than sampled analytics.
- Observability and SLOs: expose per-shard lag, spill-to-disk ratios, rebalancing frequency, and tenant throttling events into Console. Create SLOs for 99th-percentile ingest-to-availability latency and a soft SLA for maximum allowed reprocessing within a window.

Trade-offs considered: 
- Strict exactly-once semantic was rejected for now due to complexity and throughput cost; we will rely on idempotent sinks and at-least-once delivery.
- Centralized coordination vs. decentralized RAFT: chose lightweight lease service over full raft for faster failover and operational simplicity; revisit if churn increases.
- Spill-to-disk increases durability but complicates recovery; we keep spill as bounded and monitored.

Implementation plan (phase gated): 
1) Instrumentation and metrics: add per-customer event rates and partition hotness detector in router (2wk).
2) Shard-splitting controller: controller service to create virtual shards and update routing table (3wk).
3) Bounded local spill queue + backpressure markers (2wk).
4) Lease-based ownership handoff with checkpoint upload (2wk).
5) Integration test and chaos runs (1wk).
6) Canary rollout to 10% of traffic then 100% after two weeks of stable metrics.

Operational playbook: include runbook entries for high-lag incidents, manual shard split, forced reassign, and memory/disk cleanup. Document runbook in Confluence and link to alert runbooks used by SREs.

Related tickets and notes: this ticket is a design + implementation epic; several sub-tasks will be created for the controller, router changes, consumer runtime, and canary automation.

Acceptance criteria:
- No data loss for in-flight events during controlled failovers (validated by event_id diff checks),
- 95th-percentile ingest latency <= 200ms for real-time priority events during normal load,
- System maintains bounded memory under 5% of instances during 10x traffic spikes by spilling to disk or emitting backpressure markers,
- Per-tenant hotspot mitigation reduces single-partition load by at least 3x for top 1% producers.
